title: Infectious Diseases of the Genitourinary System
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)

overview.intro: This chapter covers the infections that board questions build around a genital ulcer, an abnormal discharge, a syphilis serology result, or a patient in shock with a tampon in place. It explains why chancroid hurts and a syphilitic chancre does not, how loss of lactobacilli changes vaginal chemistry, how Chlamydia and Neisseria reach and scar the upper tract, how herpes simplex virus hides in sacral ganglia, how HPV type predicts a wart or a cancer, how syphilis progresses and how its two kinds of antibody test behave, and how a superantigen causes toxic shock. Most questions hinge on one or two discriminating findings, such as pain, pH, a wet mount, or a Gram stain.
prerequisites: Gram stain, bacterial cell envelope, and endotoxin (lipooligosaccharide) structure
Vaginal and cervical epithelium, the transformation zone, and the effect of estrogen on glycogen content
Complement pathways and the membrane attack complex (C5b to C9)
MHC class II antigen presentation and T cell receptor activation
Cell cycle control by p53 and RB, and viral latency

connections.how: High-risk HPV drives the cervical, vulvar, vaginal, penile, and anal squamous lesions taught there.
Superantigens, terminal complement deficiency, and HLA-B27-associated reactive arthritis are immune mechanisms that explain toxic shock, recurrent Neisseria infection, and postinfectious arthritis.
Syphilitic aortitis is a classic cause of ascending aortic aneurysm and aortic regurgitation.
Tabes dorsalis destroys dorsal roots and dorsal columns, so its sensory signs follow the proprioceptive pathway; its pupil sign reflects a separate midbrain light reflex lesion.
Syphilis crosses the placenta, while gonorrhea, Chlamydia, and HSV infect the newborn during delivery, which predicts the timing and form of neonatal disease.

sections.title: Chancroid versus the chancre of primary syphilis

blocks.text: A genital ulcer question turns on three features: whether the ulcer hurts, the texture of its edge and base, and the behavior of the regional lymph nodes. Each feature follows from the kind of inflammation the organism provokes.

Haemophilus ducreyi is a small gram-negative coccobacillus that enters through microabrasions during intercourse. Within about a week a tender papule becomes a pustule and then breaks down into an ulcer. Bacterial toxins (including cytolethal distending toxin) and a dense neutrophil infiltrate cause necrosis, so the ulcer is painful, soft rather than indurated, with ragged undermined edges and a friable base covered by gray to yellow exudate that bleeds easily. Ulcers are often multiple because organisms spread to opposing skin.

About half of patients develop painful inguinal lymphadenitis, usually on one side, and the nodes can liquefy into buboes that rupture through the skin. On Gram stain the organisms may line up in parallel chains (described as a school of fish), and culture requires special media containing hemin (X factor).

Treponema pallidum, a thin spirochete, produces a chancre at the inoculation site after about 3 weeks (range about 10 to 90 days). Lymphocytes and plasma cells gather around small vessels whose endothelium swells and proliferates (obliterative endarteritis). Because there is little neutrophilic necrosis, the lesion is painless; because cells and fibrosis fill the base, it is firm and indurated with a smooth raised border and a clean base.

It is usually single, and the inguinal nodes enlarge on both sides but stay firm, rubbery, and nontender. The spirochete is too thin to see on Gram stain and is shown in ulcer fluid by dark-field microscopy or immunofluorescence. Serology may still be negative in the first days of the chancre (C11).

blocks.title: Genital ulcers compared
rows: Soft, ragged undermined edge, gray exudate
Grouped vesicles that become shallow erosions
Chlamydial NAAT of ulcer or node aspirate
blocks.caption: Pain separates chancroid and herpes from syphilis and LGV; ulcer texture and node behavior separate the rest.

blocks.text: Pain alone does not settle the diagnosis, because herpes is also painful, but herpes begins as grouped vesicles and leaves shallow erosions without a dirty necrotic base (C07). All genital ulcers break the mucosal barrier and recruit CD4 T cells and macrophages to the surface, which is why ulcerative infections raise both acquisition and transmission of HIV. Coinfection also occurs, so one negative test does not exclude another cause.

sections.title: Bacterial vaginosis: loss of lactobacilli and its chemical signature

blocks.text: In reproductive-age women, estrogen thickens the vaginal squamous epithelium and fills its cells with glycogen. As cells shed, glycogen is broken down to small sugars that lactobacilli ferment to lactic acid, holding vaginal pH at about 3.8 to 4.5. This acid environment, together with a stable lactobacillus population that occupies the epithelial surface, suppresses most anaerobes and gram-negative rods.

Bacterial vaginosis is a shift in the whole bacterial community rather than invasion by one pathogen. Lactobacilli decline, and Gardnerella vaginalis, a small gram-variable rod, forms a biofilm on the epithelium together with anaerobes such as Prevotella, Mobiluncus, and Atopobium vaginae. With less lactic acid, pH rises above 4.5. The anaerobes decarboxylate amino acids into volatile amines (trimethylamine, putrescine, cadaverine) that cause the fishy odor. The odor is stronger after intercourse or menses because semen and blood are alkaline, and alkali turns the amines into their volatile form. Adding 10% KOH to the discharge does the same thing on a slide, which is the positive whiff test.

Clue cells are squamous cells coated with adherent Gardnerella and anaerobes, the biofilm seen under the microscope. Because the bacteria stay on the surface and do not invade, there is little tissue injury and few neutrophils; this is why the condition is called a vaginosis rather than a vaginitis, and why itching, redness, and dysuria are usually absent. The discharge is thin, homogeneous, and gray-white, coating the vaginal walls.

blocks.title: Clinical (Amsel) criteria for bacterial vaginosis
rows: Loss of lactic acid production by lactobacilli
Clue cells (at least about 20% of epithelial cells)
blocks.caption: Three of the four findings support the diagnosis; a Gram stain scoring system (Nugent score) is the laboratory reference.

blocks.text: Risk rises with new or multiple sexual partners and douching. The condition is associated with sexual activity but is not classed as a classic sexually transmitted infection, and Gardnerella is found in many healthy women, so culturing it is not diagnostic. Enzymes from the altered flora, such as sialidases and proteases, degrade the protective mucus layer, which helps explain the associations with preterm birth, chorioamnionitis, PID, infection after gynecologic procedures, and greater susceptibility to HIV and other STIs.

sections.title: Separating the three common vaginal infections at the bedside

blocks.text: Three simple tests separate the common causes of abnormal discharge, and each measures something specific. Vaginal pH shows how much lactic acid lactobacilli are still making. The whiff test detects volatile amines produced by anaerobes. Microscopy shows the cells: a saline wet mount reveals clue cells, motile trichomonads, and neutrophils, while 10% KOH dissolves epithelial cells and leaves fungal elements intact.

Candida albicans is part of the normal flora in many women and tolerates acid, so candidal vaginitis occurs at a normal pH of 4.5 or below and produces no amines. Overgrowth follows conditions that remove competing bacteria or raise glycogen and glucose in the epithelium: broad-spectrum antibiotics, poorly controlled diabetes, pregnancy and other high-estrogen states, corticosteroids, and impaired cell-mediated immunity. Hyphae invade the superficial epithelium and provoke inflammation, so vulvar itching, burning, redness, and a thick white curdy discharge dominate.

blocks.title: Bedside findings in vaginal discharge
rows: Some neutrophils; yeast may be seen
blocks.caption: pH divides Candida from the other two; neutrophils and motile organisms divide trichomoniasis from bacterial vaginosis.

blocks.title: Reading a discharge workup
blocks.text: A woman has a malodorous discharge. pH is 5.5, so lactobacilli are no longer acidifying the vagina, which rules against Candida alone. The whiff test is positive, so anaerobes are producing amines; that fits bacterial vaginosis and is also common in trichomoniasis. The saline mount is the decider. Many squamous cells with stippled, blurred borders and very few neutrophils indicate a surface biofilm without inflammation: bacterial vaginosis. If the same slide instead showed sheets of neutrophils and pear-shaped organisms twitching with flagella, the diagnosis would be trichomoniasis. If pH had been 4.2 with a negative whiff test and itching, a KOH mount showing pseudohyphae would point to Candida.

A raised pH is not specific. Semen, menstrual blood, and atrophic vaginitis after menopause (low estrogen, little glycogen, few lactobacilli, thin inflamed epithelium) all raise it. Mixed infections occur, and a negative wet mount does not exclude trichomoniasis (C14).

sections.title: Genital Chlamydia trachomatis: a silent intracellular infection

blocks.text: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular bacterium: it depends on host ATP and nutrients and cannot grow on artificial media. Its envelope resembles a gram-negative wall but contains very little peptidoglycan, so it stains poorly on Gram stain. Serovars A to C cause trachoma, D to K cause genital and neonatal infection, and L1 to L3 cause lymphogranuloma venereum (C05).

blocks.title: Chlamydial developmental cycle
steps: Elementary body attaches to columnar epithelial cell
Endocytosed into an inclusion that avoids lysosomal fusion
Elementary body converts to reticulate body
Reticulate body divides by binary fission using host ATP
Reticulate bodies reorganize into elementary bodies
Cell lysis or extrusion releases elementary bodies to infect neighbors
blocks.caption: The cycle takes about 2 to 3 days. Only the elementary body is infectious; only the reticulate body replicates.

blocks.text: The organism infects columnar epithelium, which explains its sites: urethra, endocervix, endometrium and fallopian tubes, epididymis, rectum, and in the newborn the conjunctiva and respiratory tract. Early infection provokes little acute inflammation, so most infected women and many men have no symptoms and continue to transmit. Urethritis causes dysuria with a scant watery or mucoid discharge. Cervicitis causes a mucopurulent discharge and a friable endocervix that bleeds on contact.

Tissue damage comes mostly from the host response. Persistent or repeated infection drives lymphocyte-rich chronic inflammation, and cytokines plus immune responses to chlamydial heat shock protein 60 cause fibrosis of the tubal mucosa. Ascent causes PID (endometritis and salpingitis), with tubal-factor infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain as sequelae. Spread to the liver capsule causes perihepatitis with violin-string adhesions (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome). In men, ascent along the vas deferens causes epididymitis, the leading cause in sexually active men under about 35. Reactive arthritis is discussed with nongonococcal urethritis (C09).

A newborn delivered through an infected cervix can develop conjunctivitis 5 to 14 days after birth, with watery to mucopurulent discharge. Pneumonia appears at about 1 to 3 months: the infant is afebrile and tachypneic, with a repetitive staccato cough and often peripheral eosinophilia. Gonococcal conjunctivitis, by contrast, appears within 2 to 5 days (C06). Diagnosis in adults is by nucleic acid amplification testing; Giemsa staining of infected cells shows cytoplasmic inclusions.

sections.title: Lymphogranuloma venereum: a lymphatic chlamydial infection

blocks.text: Serovars L1, L2, and L3 differ from serovars D to K in where they grow. They infect mononuclear phagocytes and travel through lymphatics to regional nodes, so the disease is centered on lymph nodes and the tissues they drain rather than on the mucosal surface. The result is a small, brief primary lesion followed by dramatic nodal disease.

blocks.title: Stages of lymphogranuloma venereum
rows: Small painless papule, pustule, or shallow erosion that heals quickly and is often unnoticed
Local replication at the inoculation site
Painful, usually unilateral inguinal and femoral nodes with fever and malaise; nodes mat together, become fluctuant buboes, and may drain through sinuses
Spread to nodes; granulomas with central stellate abscesses
Proctocolitis: rectal pain, tenesmus, bloody mucopurulent discharge
Infection of rectal mucosa and perirectal lymphatics
blocks.caption: LGV is a disease of lymphatics: the ulcer is trivial and the nodes and their drainage beds carry the damage.

blocks.text: Inguinal nodes drain the external genitalia, so penile or vulvar inoculation produces inguinal buboes. When nodes enlarge both above and below the inguinal ligament, the ligament creates a crease between them (the groove sign). The node histology, granulomas with central stellate abscesses full of neutrophils, is shared with cat scratch disease, so it is suggestive rather than specific.

Lymph from the rectum and upper vagina drains to perirectal and deep pelvic nodes rather than inguinal nodes. After receptive anal exposure, which accounts for recent outbreaks among men who have sex with men, inguinal buboes may be absent and the presentation is proctocolitis that can mimic inflammatory bowel disease. Untreated, chronic inflammation and fibrosis of lymphatics produce strictures, fistulas, and lymphedema of the genitalia.

The contrast with chancroid is the order of events. In chancroid the painful ulcer and painful nodes are present together; in LGV the painless lesion has usually healed by the time painful buboes appear, so the patient often reports no ulcer at all. Diagnosis is by chlamydial nucleic acid testing of the lesion, rectal swab, or node aspirate, with genotyping to identify L serovars where available.

sections.title: Gonorrhea: purulent local disease, dissemination, and complement

blocks.text: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative diplococcus whose paired cocci have flattened adjacent sides. It is oxidase positive, ferments glucose but not maltose (unlike N. meningitidis), lacks a polysaccharide capsule, and is grown on selective chocolate agar (Thayer-Martin) that suppresses normal flora. Pili attach it to columnar epithelium, Opa proteins tighten that attachment, and an IgA1 protease cleaves mucosal IgA. Pili and Opa proteins change their antigens continually, so infection leaves no protective immunity and reinfection is common.

Lipooligosaccharide and peptidoglycan fragments released by the organism trigger a brisk neutrophil response. After about 2 to 7 days, men typically develop dysuria and a copious purulent urethral discharge; a Gram stain of the discharge showing gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils is highly sensitive in symptomatic men. Women are more often asymptomatic or have mild purulent cervicitis, and Gram stain of cervical secretions is far less sensitive, so nucleic acid amplification testing is used. Ascent causes PID, which tends to be more acute and febrile than chlamydial PID, and pharyngeal and rectal infection follow oral and anal exposure.

blocks.title: Gonorrhea and genital Chlamydia compared
rows: About 2 to 5 days, purulent, can perforate cornea
Disseminated infection with arthritis and pustules
blocks.caption: Both cause urethritis, cervicitis, epididymitis, and PID and frequently coexist.

blocks.text: A newborn exposed during delivery develops hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis within the first few days. Because the organism can penetrate intact corneal epithelium, untreated infection can ulcerate and perforate the cornea and cause blindness.

In a small percentage of infections, usually in women and often during menses or pregnancy, serum-resistant strains enter the blood and cause disseminated gonococcal infection. One pattern is the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome: migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis of the wrists, hands, or ankles, and a few painless pustules or vesiculopustules on an erythematous base on the extremities. The other is purulent septic monoarthritis, most often of the knee. Gonococci are the most common cause of septic arthritis in sexually active young adults.

Killing of Neisseria in blood depends heavily on the membrane attack complex (C5b to C9), which inserts into the outer membrane and lyses the cell. People with deficiency of any terminal component (C5 to C9) suffer recurrent, often disseminated Neisseria infection, most famously meningococcal but also gonococcal. Pharmacologic blockade of C5 creates the same susceptibility, which shows that the defect is in lysis rather than in opsonization or phagocytosis.

blocks.predict: A man with C8 deficiency has had two episodes of disseminated gonococcal infection. Why is he not also prone to recurrent Staphylococcus aureus infection?
blocks.explain: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall that the membrane attack complex cannot penetrate; they are cleared by C3b opsonization and phagocytosis, which work normally in terminal complement deficiency. Neisseria have a thin outer membrane that is directly lysed by C5b to C9, so only they depend on the missing step.
blocks.check: The final paragraph on the membrane attack complex.

sections.title: Genital herpes: lytic infection, latency, and neonatal risk

blocks.text: Herpes simplex virus is an enveloped double-stranded DNA virus. HSV-2 causes most recurrent genital herpes, while HSV-1, acquired through oral-genital contact, now causes a large share of first genital episodes but recurs genitally less often. The virus replicates in squamous epithelial cells, which swell, fuse into multinucleated giant cells, and develop intranuclear inclusions; loss of cell cohesion produces intraepithelial vesicles that rupture into shallow, painful erosions on a red base.

A primary infection in a person with no prior HSV antibody is the most severe episode. After about 2 to 12 days, extensive bilateral grouped vesicles appear with fever, headache, malaise, myalgia, and tender bilateral inguinal nodes. Dysuria is common, and inflammation of sacral nerve roots can cause urinary retention; some patients develop aseptic meningitis. Lesions take about 2 to 3 weeks to heal. A first episode in someone already carrying HSV-1 antibody is milder because cross-reactive immunity limits spread.

blocks.title: Herpes simplex latency and reactivation
steps: Lytic replication in genital epithelium forms vesicles
Virus enters sensory nerve endings
Retrograde axonal transport to sacral dorsal root ganglia
Latent genome persists in neurons with minimal gene expression
Stress, menses, or immunosuppression trigger reactivation
Anterograde transport returns virus to the skin
blocks.caption: Latency in sacral ganglia explains lifelong recurrence in the same dermatome and asymptomatic shedding between outbreaks.

blocks.text: Recurrences are milder because memory T cells contain them: lesions are fewer, often on one side, and heal in about a week. A prodrome of tingling or burning in the buttock, thigh, or genitals often precedes them, reflecting viral activity in the sensory neuron. Virus is also shed from normal-appearing skin, and this asymptomatic shedding accounts for much transmission. A Tzanck smear from the base of an unroofed vesicle shows multinucleated giant cells, but it cannot separate HSV-1, HSV-2, and varicella-zoster virus and is insensitive; PCR is the preferred test.

Most neonatal herpes is acquired during delivery by contact with infected genital secretions; a minority is acquired in utero or after birth. The risk is highest when the mother has a primary infection near term, because she sheds large amounts of virus, often from the cervix, and has not yet made IgG to pass across the placenta. With recurrent maternal infection the risk is low, because viral load is lower and the baby is protected by maternal antibody. Neonatal disease appears in the first weeks as skin, eye, and mouth lesions, encephalitis, or disseminated infection of the liver, lungs, and adrenals with high mortality.

sections.title: HPV: condylomata acuminata, condylomata lata, and HPV-driven carcinoma

blocks.text: Human papillomavirus is a nonenveloped double-stranded DNA virus that reaches basal keratinocytes through microabrasions. Its life cycle is tied to squamous differentiation: the genome is maintained at low copy number in basal cells, and new virions are assembled only in the maturing upper layers, which is why the cytopathic changes are seen near the surface.

Low-risk types, mainly HPV 6 and 11, cause most anogenital warts (condylomata acuminata). These are soft, flesh-colored, papillary or cauliflower-like growths on the vulva, perineum, perianal skin, vagina, cervix, and penis. Microscopically they show papillary fronds, thickened squamous epithelium, and koilocytes: superficial cells with enlarged, dark, wrinkled nuclei and a clear perinuclear halo. The same types acquired during birth can cause recurrent respiratory papillomatosis of the larynx in children.

blocks.title: Condylomata acuminata and condylomata lata
rows: Raised, papillary, cauliflower-like, often keratotic on dry skin
Plasma cell infiltrate, spirochetes on silver stain or immunostain
Rash on palms and soles, lymphadenopathy, mucous patches
blocks.caption: Both occur in warm moist anogenital skin; flat, moist lesions with a rash point to syphilis.

blocks.text: High-risk types, above all HPV 16 and 18 (also 31, 33, 45, and others), cause cancer because of two viral oncoproteins. E6 recruits a host ubiquitin ligase that degrades p53, so damaged cells neither arrest nor die. E7 binds RB and releases E2F transcription factors, pushing cells into S phase. In low-risk types these proteins bind weakly and the genome usually stays episomal. In high-risk infections the genome often integrates into host DNA and disrupts the viral E2 gene that normally restrains E6 and E7, so their expression rises. Most infections are cleared by cell-mediated immunity within about 1 to 2 years; persistence is the key risk.

blocks.title: From high-risk HPV infection to carcinoma
steps: High-risk HPV infects basal cells at a transformation zone
Persistent infection escapes immune clearance
Integration disrupts E2, increasing E6 and E7
E6 degrades p53; E7 inactivates RB
Unchecked proliferation accumulates host mutations
Intraepithelial neoplasia progresses to invasive squamous carcinoma
blocks.caption: Overexpression of the host protein p16 is a tissue marker of this E7-driven pathway.

blocks.text: High-risk HPV causes nearly all cervical carcinomas, most anal carcinomas, a large share of vaginal carcinomas, the HPV-related subset of vulvar and penile carcinomas in younger patients, and a growing share of oropharyngeal carcinomas of the tonsil and base of tongue, mostly HPV 16. The squamocolumnar junctions of the cervix and anus are vulnerable because their immature metaplastic cells are easily infected and actively dividing (RE-13-J).

Urethritis is inflammation of the urethra, causing dysuria and urethral discharge or itching. It is called nongonococcal when urethral secretions contain neutrophils but no intracellular gram-negative diplococci and gonococcal testing is negative. Compared with gonorrhea, onset is slower and discharge is scant, clear, or mucoid, because these organisms provoke a milder neutrophil response.

blocks.title: Causes of nongonococcal urethritis
rows: Most common identified cause; also epididymitis and reactive arthritis
Tiny bacterium with no cell wall, invisible on Gram stain
Important cause of persistent or recurrent urethritis
Often found in healthy people; causal role less certain
No organism is found in many cases
blocks.caption: Because Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma lack a cell wall, they are not seen on Gram stain and are unaffected by agents that act on peptidoglycan.

blocks.text: Reactive arthritis is a sterile inflammatory arthritis that begins about 1 to 4 weeks after an infection elsewhere, either genitourinary (Chlamydia most often) or enteric (Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter). The classic triad is arthritis, conjunctivitis (sometimes anterior uveitis), and urethritis, although many patients do not show all three. The arthritis is asymmetric and involves a few large joints of the legs, often with enthesitis of the Achilles tendon or plantar fascia, dactylitis (sausage digits), and sometimes sacroiliitis. Skin and mucosal signs include thick hyperkeratotic plaques on the palms and soles (keratoderma blennorrhagicum), circinate balanitis, and painless oral ulcers. Post-urethritis cases occur mainly in young men.

Joint fluid is inflammatory but culture is sterile, which separates reactive arthritis from disseminated gonococcal infection, where organisms reach the joint and pustules appear on the skin. The mechanism involves bacterial antigens, and in Chlamydia even viable but nonculturable organisms, carried to the synovium in monocytes, together with an abnormal host response. HLA-B27, an MHC class I allele, increases the risk and the likelihood of severe, chronic, or axial disease, possibly by presenting bacterial peptides that resemble self peptides to CD8 T cells or by misfolding in a way that triggers IL-23 and IL-17 driven inflammation. Rheumatoid factor is negative, which places reactive arthritis among the seronegative spondyloarthropathies with ankylosing spondylitis and psoriatic arthritis.

sections.title: Stages of syphilis and the endarteritis behind them

blocks.text: Treponema pallidum is a thin, tightly coiled spirochete that moves by corkscrew motion and cannot be grown on routine media. Its outer membrane has few exposed proteins, which slows antibody recognition and lets it persist for decades. It spreads by sexual contact and across the placenta. In every stage, the basic lesion is obliterative endarteritis with a plasma cell rich infiltrate, and where the organism has spread determines what that lesion damages.

blocks.title: Natural history of untreated syphilis
steps: Inoculation through mucosa or broken skin
Primary: painless chancre after about 3 weeks, heals in weeks
Spirochetemia spreads organisms throughout the body
Secondary: rash, condylomata lata, lymphadenopathy, weeks to months later
Latent: positive serology without signs
Tertiary in a minority: gummas, aortitis, neurosyphilis after years
blocks.caption: Early stages are rich in organisms and infectious; tertiary lesions have few organisms and reflect the host response.

blocks.text: The chancre heals in about 3 to 6 weeks even without treatment, because organisms have already disseminated. Secondary syphilis appears about 2 to 10 weeks after the chancre, when blood-borne spread seeds the skin and mucosa. It produces a symmetric, nonpruritic, reddish-brown maculopapular rash on the trunk and extremities that characteristically includes the palms and soles, condylomata lata in moist skin, gray mucous patches in the mouth, generalized painless lymphadenopathy, fever, malaise, and patchy hair loss. Less often there is hepatitis, immune complex glomerulonephritis, or early neurosyphilis such as meningitis or ocular involvement. These lesions are full of spirochetes, so secondary syphilis is the most infectious stage.

Latent syphilis has positive serology but no signs. Early latent disease (infection within about the past year) can still relapse into secondary lesions. Untreated, a minority of patients, historically about one third, develop tertiary disease years to decades later.

blocks.title: Tertiary syphilis lesions
rows: Delayed hypersensitivity granuloma with central necrosis and few organisms
Firm, rubbery destructive masses in skin, bone, liver, testis
Endarteritis of the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta and arch, ischemic loss of medial elastic tissue
Wrinkled tree-bark intima, ascending aortic aneurysm, aortic root dilation with aortic regurgitation, coronary ostial narrowing
Degeneration of lumbosacral dorsal roots and dorsal columns
Loss of proprioception and vibration, sensory ataxia, positive Romberg sign, lightning pains, areflexia, Charcot joints, Argyll Robertson pupils
blocks.caption: The thoracic aorta is affected because its wall depends on a dense network of vasa vasorum; the abdominal aorta has few and is usually spared.

blocks.text: Tabes dorsalis shows how anatomy predicts signs. Large-fiber proprioceptive axons in the dorsal roots and dorsal columns are lost, so the patient cannot sense joint position, walks with a broad-based stamping gait, and falls when the eyes close (Romberg sign). Loss of the afferent limb abolishes deep tendon reflexes, and unfelt joint trauma destroys joints. Argyll Robertson pupils are small and irregular, constrict to accommodation, but do not react to light, a sign attributed to a lesion of the light reflex pathway near the pretectal midbrain.

sections.title: Syphilis serology: nontreponemal and treponemal tests

blocks.text: Because T. pallidum cannot be cultured routinely, syphilis is diagnosed mostly by two families of antibody test that measure different things. Nontreponemal tests, the VDRL and the RPR, detect IgM and IgG against a cardiolipin, lecithin, and cholesterol antigen. Cardiolipin is a phospholipid of mitochondrial membranes released from damaged host cells and also present in treponemal membranes, so these antibodies are a marker of tissue injury rather than of the organism itself.

Results are titers from twofold dilutions, and a fourfold change is significant. Titers become positive about 1 to 4 weeks after the chancre appears, so they can be negative in early primary syphilis. They peak in secondary syphilis, when sensitivity approaches 100%, fall after successful treatment and may become nonreactive, and decline slowly in untreated late disease. In secondary syphilis a very high antibody concentration can prevent the antigen lattice from forming in undiluted serum, giving a false negative that disappears on dilution (the prozone phenomenon).

Because anticardiolipin antibodies arise whenever tissue is injured or autoimmunity is active, nontreponemal tests have biologic false positives: pregnancy, systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid syndrome, acute viral infections such as infectious mononucleosis, hepatitis, varicella, and HIV, as well as malaria, leprosy, injection drug use, and older age.

Treponemal tests, including the fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test (FTA-ABS), the T. pallidum particle agglutination assay (TP-PA), and automated enzyme or chemiluminescence immunoassays, detect antibody to T. pallidum antigens. They are more specific and turn positive at about the same time or slightly earlier, but in most patients they remain positive for life even after cure. They therefore confirm that infection has occurred but cannot show whether it is active or follow treatment. Cross-reactions occur with other treponemes (yaws, pinta, bejel) and sometimes with Lyme disease.

blocks.title: The two families of syphilis tests
blocks.caption: One family tracks disease activity; the other records lifetime exposure.

blocks.title: Interpreting paired syphilis results
blocks.text: Pattern 1: RPR reactive at 1:64, treponemal test reactive. Both antibodies are present and the high titer signals activity, so this is untreated or recently treated syphilis. Pattern 2: RPR reactive at 1:2, treponemal test nonreactive. Anticardiolipin antibody without antibody to the organism is a biologic false positive; in a pregnant woman or a patient with lupus this is expected. Pattern 3: RPR nonreactive, treponemal test reactive. The person has been infected at some point; the usual explanation is past treated syphilis, but very early primary infection and untreated late disease, when nontreponemal titers wane, are alternatives. A painless chancre with both tests negative is still possible syphilis, because antibodies lag behind the lesion; dark-field examination of the ulcer can show spirochetes.
In the cerebrospinal fluid, a reactive VDRL is highly specific for neurosyphilis but often negative in true disease, so a negative result does not exclude it.

Treponema pallidum crosses the placenta at any stage of pregnancy, and the risk of transmission is highest when the mother has primary, secondary, or early latent syphilis, the stages with the most spirochetes in her blood. Infection can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, hydrops fetalis, prematurity, or neonatal death. Many infected infants look normal at birth and develop signs over the following weeks. The placenta is often large and pale with villitis and endarteritis of villous vessels.

The findings divide by timing. Early congenital syphilis, appearing in the first 2 years, reflects active infection with abundant organisms. Late congenital syphilis, appearing after 2 years, reflects scarring and maldevelopment of tissues injured during infancy and persistent low-grade inflammation, and its signs are therefore permanent.

blocks.title: Findings in congenital syphilis
rows: Infected nasal mucosa; discharge full of spirochetes and infectious
Rash, often on palms and soles, with peeling or bullae
Hematogenous spread to liver, spleen, and nodes
Painful limbs with reluctance to move
Osteochondritis and periostitis of long bones
Destruction of nasal cartilage and bone after rhinitis
Damaged tooth buds; notched, widely spaced, peg-shaped upper central incisors
Damaged first molar buds with many small poorly formed cusps
Chronic periostitis causing anterior bowing of the tibia
Damage to the eighth cranial nerve and inner ear
blocks.caption: Hutchinson teeth, interstitial keratitis, and eighth nerve deafness together form the Hutchinson triad; other late signs include frontal bossing, perioral scars (rhagades), and painless knee effusions.

blocks.text: The dental findings show the importance of timing. The crowns of the permanent incisors and first molars calcify during infancy, the period when early congenital infection is active, so inflammation around the developing tooth buds leaves deformities that are seen only years later when these teeth erupt.

Serologic diagnosis in the newborn is complicated by maternal IgG, which crosses the placenta, so a positive test in the infant may only reflect the mother. A nontreponemal titer fourfold or more above the mother's, or IgM antibody, which cannot cross the placenta, indicates that the infant itself is infected. Passively acquired antibody falls over the first months of life.

sections.title: Toxic shock syndrome: a superantigen disease

blocks.text: A conventional protein antigen activates only the rare T cell clones whose receptors fit one processed peptide in the MHC groove, well under 0.01% of T cells. A superantigen skips processing. Toxic shock syndrome toxin 1 (TSST-1) from Staphylococcus aureus binds the outside of MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells and the V beta region of the T cell receptor directly, so every T cell with a matching V beta family is activated, up to about 20% of all T cells.

blocks.title: From superantigen to shock
steps: S. aureus grows locally and secretes TSST-1
Toxin crosses mucosa into blood
TSST-1 bridges MHC class II and T cell receptor V beta
Polyclonal T cell activation releases IL-2 and IFN-gamma
Macrophages release TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6
Vasodilation and capillary leak cause fever, hypotension, organ injury
blocks.caption: The organism stays local; the toxin and the cytokine storm it triggers are systemic.

blocks.text: Menstrual toxic shock syndrome is linked to high-absorbency tampons, especially when left in place, which introduce oxygen and create a near-neutral, protein-rich environment that favors toxin production. Nonmenstrual cases follow nasal packing after surgery, surgical and burn wounds, postpartum and post-abortion infection, and skin and soft tissue infections. TSST-1 causes nearly all menstrual cases, while staphylococcal enterotoxins, especially B, cause many nonmenstrual cases. Most adults have neutralizing antibody to TSST-1, so disease occurs mainly in people who lack it.

blocks.title: Features of staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome
rows: IL-1 and TNF reset the hypothalamic set point
Palms and soles, about 1 to 2 weeks after onset
Systolic pressure 90 mmHg or lower in adults
Vomiting or diarrhea, myalgia with high creatine kinase, mucosal hyperemia, raised creatinine, raised bilirubin or transaminases, platelets below 100,000 per microliter, confusion
blocks.caption: Thresholds follow the standard surveillance case definition.

blocks.text: Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, caused by Streptococcus pyogenes pyrogenic exotoxins that also act as superantigens, differs mainly in source and invasiveness. It usually arises from deep soft tissue infection such as necrotizing fasciitis, often with severe local pain, and blood cultures are frequently positive.

blocks.predict: A woman with menstrual toxic shock has profound hypotension, yet her blood cultures grow nothing. How can a local infection produce this?
blocks.explain: The S. aureus remains in the vagina on the tampon. Only TSST-1 enters the blood, and because it activates a large fraction of all T cells without antigen processing, a small amount of toxin triggers a systemic release of IL-2, IFN-gamma, TNF, and IL-1 that dilates vessels and causes capillary leak.
blocks.check: The superantigen paragraph and the flow figure.

blocks.text: Trichomonas vaginalis is an anaerobic, pear-shaped flagellated protozoan with four anterior flagella and an undulating membrane. It exists only as a trophozoite and forms no cyst, so it cannot survive long outside the body and is transmitted almost entirely by sexual contact. It infects the squamous epithelium of the vagina and ectocervix, and the urethra and occasionally the prostate in men. It is the most common nonviral sexually transmitted infection worldwide.

The organism attaches to epithelial cells with surface adhesins and damages them by contact-dependent cytotoxicity and secreted cysteine proteases. The injured epithelium releases chemoattractants, and neutrophils flood the vagina. Inflammation of the ectocervix produces punctate subepithelial hemorrhages, the strawberry cervix; it is seen with the naked eye in only a small fraction of patients and more often on colposcopy. The infection disturbs the lactobacillus population, so pH rises above 4.5 and the whiff test is often positive.

Women develop a frothy, yellow-green, malodorous discharge with vulvovaginal itching and irritation, dysuria, and pain with intercourse, although many are asymptomatic. Most infected men have no symptoms and act as carriers; some have nongonococcal urethritis (C09). Infection does not produce lasting immunity, so reinfection from an untreated partner is common.

blocks.title: Trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis, both with pH above 4.5
blocks.caption: Neutrophils and motile organisms mark the inflammatory infection; clue cells without neutrophils mark the flora shift.

blocks.text: On a saline wet mount, trophozoites are about the size of a neutrophil or slightly larger and move with a jerky, twitching motion. Motility fades within minutes as the specimen cools and dries, and the wet mount detects only about half to two thirds of infections, so nucleic acid amplification tests are preferred when available. Organisms may also be reported on a Pap smear. Infection in pregnancy is associated with preterm rupture of membranes, preterm birth, and low birth weight, and the mucosal inflammation and microulceration increase both acquisition and transmission of HIV.

integration.text: Anatomy and microbiology explain where each infection settles. Gonococci and Chlamydia attach to columnar epithelium, so they target the endocervix, urethra, and tubes and ascend to cause PID; Trichomonas and Candida favor stratified squamous epithelium of the vagina; HPV needs dividing basal cells at a transformation zone; LGV serovars and H. ducreyi reach regional nodes, whose drainage pattern predicts inguinal buboes or rectal disease. Lymphatic and venous drainage, placental transfer, and passage through the birth canal decide whether neonatal infection is congenital (syphilis) or acquired at delivery (gonorrhea, Chlamydia, HSV).

Immunology and pathology explain most of the clinical picture. The difference between a painful neutrophilic ulcer and a painless plasma cell rich chancre, between a vaginosis with few neutrophils and a vaginitis with many, and between local infection and toxic shock is the host response. Antigenic variation explains gonococcal reinfection, terminal complement deficiency explains disseminated Neisseria, HLA-B27 shapes reactive arthritis, and the persistence of treponemal antibodies explains why only nontreponemal titers track activity. Bedside tests narrow the diagnosis, but each has limits: wet mounts miss trichomonads, serology lags behind early chancres, and coinfection is common, so one positive finding should prompt a search for others.

summary: Chancroid (H. ducreyi) gives a painful, soft, ragged ulcer with gray exudate and suppurative nodes; primary syphilis gives a painless, indurated, clean chancre with rubbery nontender nodes.
Bacterial vaginosis is replacement of lactobacilli by Gardnerella and anaerobes: thin gray discharge, pH above 4.5, positive whiff test from amines, clue cells, few neutrophils.
pH separates Candida (normal pH, pseudohyphae on KOH) from bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis; neutrophils and motile trophozoites separate trichomoniasis from bacterial vaginosis.

C. trachomatis cycles between infectious elementary bodies and replicating reticulate bodies, is often silent, and scars the tubes through the immune response; neonatal conjunctivitis precedes afebrile staccato pneumonia.
LGV (L1 to L3) is lymphatic: a trivial painless lesion, then painful buboes or proctocolitis, and late strictures or elephantiasis.

Gonorrhea causes purulent urethritis with intracellular gram-negative diplococci, PID, hyperacute neonatal conjunctivitis, and disseminated arthritis with tenosynovitis and pustules; C5 to C9 deficiency predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infection.
HSV forms painful grouped vesicles with multinucleated giant cells, hides in sacral ganglia, and is most dangerous to the newborn when the mother acquires primary infection near delivery.
HPV 6 and 11 cause condylomata acuminata with koilocytes; high-risk HPV 16 and 18 use E6 against p53 and E7 against RB to cause anogenital and oropharyngeal carcinoma.

Syphilis progresses from chancre to a palm and sole rash with condylomata lata, to latency, and in a minority to gummas, ascending aortitis, and tabes dorsalis; VDRL and RPR titers track activity, while treponemal tests stay positive for life.

Toxic shock syndrome is TSST-1 bridging MHC class II and T cell receptor V beta, causing a cytokine storm with fever, hypotension, erythroderma, later palm and sole desquamation, and usually negative blood cultures.

verify: Incubation periods (chancroid about 4 to 10 days, syphilis about 10 to 90 days, gonorrhea about 2 to 7 days, HSV about 2 to 12 days, LGV primary lesion about 3 to 30 days) are approximate and vary among sources.

Percentages are approximate and vary among sources: the share of chancroid patients with lymphadenitis, the proportion of untreated syphilis progressing to tertiary disease (historically about one third), the sensitivity of the wet mount for Trichomonas, the frequency of disseminated gonococcal infection, and the proportion of reactive arthritis patients who are HLA-B27 positive.

Neonatal HSV transmission risk with primary versus recurrent maternal infection is quoted differently between sources (roughly 30% to 50% versus 1% to 3% or less); confirm the figures NABNE expects if tested.
The fraction of patients whose treponemal tests revert to nonreactive after early treatment varies among studies; the chapter states only that most stay positive for life.
Taxonomy: Atopobium vaginae has been reclassified as Fannyhessea vaginae, and Gardnerella vaginalis has been split into several species; confirm which names NABNE uses.
The causal role of Ureaplasma urealyticum in urethritis is debated; the chapter lists it as in the objective but notes the uncertainty.

Toxic shock syndrome thresholds (fever 38.9 °C (102 °F), systolic pressure 90 mmHg or lower, platelets below 100,000 per microliter, three or more organ systems) follow the CDC surveillance case definition; confirm the current version.
The Amsel clue cell threshold (at least about 20% of epithelial cells) and the neutrophil threshold for diagnosing urethritis on Gram stain differ slightly among guidelines.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Fitz-Hugh-Curtis, Argyll Robertson, Hutchinson, Amsel, and Nugent, and the descriptive terms school of fish and groove sign.
